decks.title: Water Resources — Part 1: Sources, conservation and rainwater harvesting
goals: Distinguish surface water from groundwater with examples
Explain why water conservation is needed in India
Describe rooftop rainwater harvesting and explain how it recharges groundwater

slides.heading: Water: plenty, yet scarce
slides.body_md: Part 1 — India receives a great deal of rain, yet many towns queue for tankers in May and many villages see their wells run dry. The answer lies in **where**, **when** and **how** water is found and used.

rows: Lakes of Kashmir, tanks of Tamil Nadu
Wells and tube wells of the Ganga plain

visual.alt: Table of sources of fresh water with type and example

slides.narration: Namaste! India gets plenty of rain in the monsoon, yet many towns wait for water tankers in summer and wells in many villages dry up. Why? Water is not spread evenly through the country or through the year, and we often use it carelessly. In this part we look at where our water comes from, why we must conserve it, and how we can harvest the rain.

slides.heading: Surface water and groundwater
slides.body_md: **Surface water** is water on the surface of the land: **rivers, lakes, ponds, tanks and reservoirs**. It is fed by rain and, in the north, by melting snow. **Groundwater** is water that has **soaked into the ground** and fills the pores and cracks of rocks below the **water table**, in layers called **aquifers**. It is drawn up through **wells** and **tube wells** and is renewed (**recharged**) when rain soaks in.

slides.narration: Surface water is the water we can see: rivers, lakes, ponds, tanks and reservoirs. Groundwater is hidden. Rain soaks into the ground and fills the tiny spaces in soil and rock below a level called the water table. Rock layers that hold this water are called aquifers. We reach groundwater with wells and tube wells, and it is refilled when rain soaks in again.

slides.heading: Where India’s water is found
slides.body_md: **Northern plains:** large **perennial rivers** fed by Himalayan snow and monsoon rain; thick, porous **alluvium** stores plenty of **groundwater**, close to the surface. **Peninsular plateau:** rivers are **rain-fed** and shrink in the dry season; hard, **impervious crystalline rocks** hold little groundwater, so water is stored in **tanks** and reservoirs. **Western Rajasthan:** scanty rain, few rivers, deep and often salty groundwater. **Coasts and the north-east:** heavy rain, but much of it runs off quickly to the sea.

visual.alt: Table comparing surface water and groundwater in three regions of India

slides.narration: Water is not shared evenly. The northern plains have big rivers fed by Himalayan snow, and their deep, porous soil holds a lot of groundwater close to the surface. On the peninsular plateau the rivers depend on rain and shrink in the dry season, and the hard rock holds little groundwater, so people store water in tanks. Western Rajasthan has very little water of either kind.

slides.heading: Quick check: surface or groundwater?
slides.body_md: Classify a source of water.
slides.narration: Quick check. Rivers, lakes and tanks are surface water; water below the water table is groundwater.

slides.heading: Why water must be conserved
slides.body_md: **Uneven in time:** most rain falls in **three to four monsoon months**; the rest of the year is dry. **Uneven in space:** the north-east and west coast are very wet, Rajasthan and the rain-shadow Deccan dry. **Rising demand:** a growing population, expanding **irrigation**, industries and cities. **Over-use of groundwater:** water tables are falling in parts of Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. **Pollution** of rivers and lakes by sewage, industrial waste and farm chemicals reduces usable water. **Droughts** recur when the monsoon fails.

visual.alt: Flow of four causes joining to make water conservation necessary

slides.narration: Why must we save water? Most of our rain falls in just a few monsoon months, and some regions get far less than others. Meanwhile, more people, more farms, more factories and bigger cities all need more water. In many districts pumps draw groundwater faster than rain can refill it, so the water table keeps falling. And polluted rivers and lakes cannot be used safely.

slides.heading: Worked example: a falling water table
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In a district of central Punjab, farmers have to deepen their tube wells every few years, though canals and rivers flow nearby. Explain why, and suggest two remedies.

**Step 1. Demand.** Water-hungry crops such as rice and sugarcane are grown, often in the dry season too.

**Step 2. Pumping.** Thousands of powerful pumps draw water day and night; cheap electricity encourages over-use.

**Step 3. Recharge.** Recharge from rain is far smaller than the water pumped out, so the water table drops year after year.

**Remedies.** Switch some area to less thirsty crops; use **drip or sprinkler** irrigation; build **recharge pits** and check dams to harvest rain.

visual.alt: Flow showing how heavy pumping for thirsty crops makes the water table fall

slides.narration: Why must Punjab farmers keep deepening their tube wells? Rice and sugarcane need a great deal of water, and powerful pumps run for long hours. Rain refills the ground far more slowly than the pumps empty it, so the water table sinks every year. Growing less thirsty crops, using drip or sprinkler irrigation and building recharge pits can help the water table recover.

slides.heading: Quick check: need for conservation
slides.body_md: Identify a reason for water scarcity.
slides.narration: Quick check. When pumping is faster than recharge, the water table falls.

slides.heading: Rainwater harvesting: meaning and methods
slides.body_md: **Rainwater harvesting** is collecting and storing rainwater where it falls, either for **direct use** or to **recharge groundwater**. **Methods:** **rooftop harvesting** into tanks or recharge pits; **recharge pits, trenches and wells** that let runoff soak in; **check dams** and **percolation tanks** across small streams; **farm ponds**; reviving **traditional village tanks and ponds**. It is simple, cheap and can be done by every household, school, office and village.

visual.alt: Table of rainwater harvesting methods with where they are used and how they help

slides.narration: Rainwater harvesting means catching the rain where it falls and keeping it, either to use or to let it soak into the ground. Rain can be collected from roofs into tanks or recharge pits. Pits and trenches let runoff soak in. Small check dams slow streams so water seeps into the ground, and farm ponds store runoff for crops. Even old village tanks can be cleaned and used again.

slides.heading: Rooftop rainwater harvesting
slides.body_md: Rain falling on a **roof** is led by **gutters** into a **down pipe**. A **first-flush** device throws away the dirty first rain; a **filter** of sand and gravel cleans the rest. The water goes to a **storage tank** for use, and the **overflow** goes into a **recharge pit** or an old well, from which it **percolates** down to the **aquifer**, raising the **water table**. Every millimetre of rain on one square metre of roof gives about one litre of water.

slides.narration: Here is how rooftop harvesting works. Rain on the roof runs into gutters and a down pipe. The first rain, which washes dust off the roof, is thrown away. The rest passes through a filter of sand and gravel into a storage tank. When the tank is full, the overflow goes into a recharge pit, where it slowly soaks down and refills the groundwater. One millimetre of rain on one square metre gives about one litre.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much rain can a roof catch?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A dairy cooperative near Anand has a shed roof of 300 m². The area gets about 800 mm of rain a year, and about 80% of the rain on the roof can be collected (runoff coefficient 0.8). How much water can it harvest in a year? (Illustrative figures.)

**Step 1. Rule.** Litres harvested = roof area (m²) × rainfall (mm) × runoff coefficient.

**Step 2.** $300 \times 800 \times 0.8 = 192000$ litres.

**Step 3. Interpret.** That is 192 cubic metres a year — enough to wash the sheds for many months or, through a recharge pit, to raise the local water table.

visual.alt: Table of the illustrative figures and the harvest for a shed roof

slides.narration: Let us estimate the harvest from a dairy shed roof. Multiply the roof area, three hundred square metres, by the yearly rainfall, eight hundred millimetres, and then by the share of rain that can be collected, about four fifths. The answer is one hundred and ninety two thousand litres in a year. Stored or sent into a recharge pit, that water makes a real difference.

slides.heading: Why rainwater harvesting matters
slides.body_md: **Importance:** it **raises the water table** and revives dried wells and handpumps; provides water in the **dry season**; reduces dependence on distant rivers and tankers; reduces **flooding of streets** and drains in cities, since less water runs off; reduces **soil erosion**; **dilutes** fluoride and salts in groundwater, improving its quality; is **low-cost** and needs little energy; and involves **people** in managing their own water. Several states and cities have made rooftop harvesting a condition for new buildings.

visual.alt: Flow showing how harvesting rain reduces runoff, recharges groundwater and reduces urban flooding

slides.narration: Rainwater harvesting helps in many ways. It refills groundwater, so dried wells and handpumps start working again. It gives water in the dry season and cuts the need for tankers. In cities, less water rushes into the streets, so there is less flooding. It also improves the quality of groundwater, costs little, and lets ordinary people take charge of their own water.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Surface water flows in rivers and stands in lakes and tanks; groundwater lies below the water table and is reached by wells. The northern plains are rich in both, the peninsula much less. We must conserve water because rain is seasonal and uneven, demand is rising and groundwater is over used. Rainwater harvesting stores rain and refills the ground.

decks.title: Water Resources — Part 2: Irrigation
goals: Explain why irrigation is needed in India
Explain why tank irrigation is common in peninsular India and tube wells in the northern plains
Compare perennial and inundation canals and state disadvantages of canal irrigation
Explain how drip and sprinkler irrigation save water

slides.heading: Water for the fields
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **irrigation** is the artificial supply of water to crops. It turned the dry fields of Punjab into India’s granary and lets farmers in Tamil Nadu grow a second crop. India uses several methods, each suited to its region.

rows: Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, river deltas

visual.alt: Table of irrigation methods and typical regions

slides.narration: Irrigation means giving water to crops by artificial means instead of waiting for rain. It made Punjab the granary of India and lets farmers in many states grow two or three crops a year. India waters its fields with wells and tube wells, tanks, canals, and newer methods such as drip and sprinkler irrigation. Each suits a particular kind of land and water supply.

slides.heading: Why irrigation is needed in India
slides.body_md: **Seasonal rain:** most rain falls in three to four months; rabi crops grow in the dry winter. **Uncertain monsoon:** onset may be late, with long breaks or failure. **Uneven rain:** large areas such as Rajasthan, Gujarat and the rain-shadow Deccan get too little. **Thirsty crops:** rice, sugarcane and jute need much more water than rain gives in many areas. **Multiple cropping and high-yielding seeds** need an assured water supply. **Porous soils** such as sandy and red soils do not hold water.

rows: Breaks in July harm young rice

visual.alt: Table of reasons for irrigation with an example of each

slides.narration: Why do Indian farmers need irrigation? Most rain falls in a few monsoon months, but crops such as wheat grow in the dry winter. The monsoon is uncertain: it may come late or stop for weeks. Some regions get very little rain. Crops like rice and sugarcane need a lot of water, and high yielding seeds need water on time. Sandy and red soils also lose water quickly.

slides.heading: Wells and tube wells
slides.body_md: **Wells** are pits dug down to the water table; water is lifted by hand, by the **Persian wheel** or by pumps. They are cheap, simple and owned by individual farmers, but irrigate small areas and may dry up. **Tube wells** are deep, narrow holes **bored** into the aquifer, with a pipe and an **electric or diesel pump**; they can lift large amounts of water from great depths. Wells and tube wells together are the **leading source of irrigation in India (as of the early 2020s)**, especially in **Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat** and parts of Rajasthan.

visual.alt: Flow from aquifer recharge to tube well and pump to water on demand

slides.narration: A well is a pit dug down to the water table, from which water is lifted by hand, by an animal turning a Persian wheel, or by a pump. Wells are cheap and belong to the farmer, but they water only a small area. A tube well is a deep, narrow bore with a powerful electric or diesel pump. Wells and tube wells are now the biggest source of irrigation in India.

slides.heading: Worked example: why tube wells suit the northern plains
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give geographical reasons why tube wells are the main source of irrigation in western Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.

**Step 1. Soil.** Deep, soft **alluvium** is easy and cheap to bore through.

**Step 2. Water.** The porous alluvium stores plenty of **groundwater**, recharged by monsoon rain and by **perennial Himalayan rivers** and canals; the water table was high.

**Step 3. Power and land.** Rural **electricity** is widely available; the land is **flat**, so water spreads easily.

**Step 4. Demand.** Fertile soil, dense farming and high-yielding wheat and rice create a large, year-round demand for water.

visual.alt: Flow of four reasons leading to widespread tube wells in the northern plains

slides.narration: Why are tube wells so common in Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh? The soft, deep alluvium is easy to drill. It holds a lot of groundwater, refilled by monsoon rain and by snow fed rivers and canals. Electricity reaches most villages, and the flat land lets water spread easily. And the fertile soil and intensive farming of wheat and rice create a huge demand for water.

slides.heading: Quick check: wells and tube wells
slides.body_md: Explain where tube wells suit best.
slides.narration: Quick check. Soft alluvium with plentiful groundwater suits tube wells.

slides.heading: Tank irrigation
slides.body_md: A **tank** is a natural or man-made depression, often made by building an **earthen embankment** across a small stream, that stores **rainwater** for irrigation. **Where:** **Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh** (and parts of Odisha, Madhya Pradesh). **Why in the peninsula:** hard, **impervious rock** lets little water percolate, so groundwater is scarce and wells are hard to dig; rivers are **rain-fed and seasonal**, unfit for perennial canals; **undulating land** has natural hollows, making tanks easy to build; rain is concentrated in a short season and must be stored; small, scattered fields. **Drawbacks:** tanks **dry up** in long dry spells; they **silt up**; much water is lost by **evaporation**; they occupy fertile land and irrigate small areas.

rows: No water for canals in the dry season

visual.alt: Table of reasons why tank irrigation is common in peninsular India

slides.narration: A tank is a hollow, natural or made by building an earth bank across a small stream, that stores rainwater. Tanks are common in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. There, the hard rock holds little groundwater, the rivers dry up after the rains, and the rolling land has many natural hollows to store water. But tanks can dry up, fill with silt and lose water to evaporation.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading irrigation data
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two illustrative districts irrigate their fields as shown (share of net irrigated area). Which is more likely to be on the Deccan plateau of Tamil Nadu, and which on the Ganga plain? Give reasons.

| Source | District A | District B |
|---|---|---|
| Wells and tube wells | 72% | 30% |
| Canals | 24% | 18% |
| Tanks | 1% | 42% |
| Other | 3% | 10% |

**District A:** wells and tube wells dominate (72%), tanks almost absent → **Ganga plain**: soft alluvium, rich groundwater.

**District B:** tanks are the largest source (42%) → **Tamil Nadu plateau**: hard rock, seasonal rivers, natural hollows.

**Check.** Each column adds to $72 + 24 + 1 + 3 = 100$.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative irrigation shares in two districts

slides.narration: Compare the two imagined districts. In District A, wells and tube wells water nearly three quarters of the land and tanks hardly matter. That fits the Ganga plain, with its soft soil and rich groundwater. In District B, tanks are the biggest source. That fits the Tamil Nadu plateau, where hard rock holds little groundwater and rain must be stored in tanks.

slides.body_md: Explain why tanks suit the peninsula.
slides.narration: Quick check. Hard rock and seasonal rivers make tanks the best way to store rain.

slides.heading: Canal irrigation: inundation and perennial canals
slides.body_md: **Inundation canals** are taken straight from a river **without a barrage**; water enters only when the river is **in flood** during the rainy season, so they are unreliable. **Perennial canals** are taken from a river through a **barrage, weir or dam**, which holds the water up so the canal flows **all year**. Perennial canals are found mainly in **Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh** and the **deltas** of the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, where land is flat, soil is deep and rivers carry water all year. Examples: the **Indira Gandhi Canal** (Rajasthan), the **Upper Ganga Canal**, the **Western Yamuna Canal**, the **Sirhind Canal**.

slides.narration: An inundation canal is cut from a river without any barrage, so water flows into it only when the river is in flood, during the rains. A perennial canal starts at a barrage, weir or dam that holds the river water high, so the canal flows all year. Perennial canals irrigate the flat plains of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and the deltas of the south, such as the Kaveri delta.

slides.heading: Disadvantages of canal irrigation
slides.body_md: **Waterlogging:** over-irrigation and seepage from unlined canals raise the water table to the surface. **Salinity and alkalinity:** as waterlogged land dries, salts rise and form a white crust (called **reh** or **kallar**), making land barren. **Disease:** stagnant water breeds **mosquitoes** (malaria). **Wastage:** much water is lost by **seepage and evaporation**. **Cost:** canals are expensive to build and maintain, and suit only **flat** land. **Unfairness:** farms at the **tail end** may get little water.

visual.alt: Flow showing how over-irrigation by canals leads to waterlogging and saline land

slides.narration: Canals have problems too. When fields are over watered and unlined canals leak, the water table rises until the land is waterlogged. As it dries, salts come up and form a white crust that makes the soil barren. Standing water breeds mosquitoes. Much water is lost on the way through seepage and evaporation, and farms at the far end of a canal may get very little.

slides.heading: Modern methods: drip and sprinkler irrigation
slides.body_md: **Drip irrigation:** water flows through a network of pipes and comes out **drop by drop** from emitters at the **root zone** of each plant. Very little is lost to **evaporation, runoff or weeds**; fertiliser can be mixed in the water. Suits **orchards, sugarcane, vegetables, grapes and cotton** in dry areas such as **Maharashtra, Karnataka and Rajasthan**. **Sprinkler irrigation:** water is pumped through pipes and **sprayed like rain** by rotating nozzles. Suits **uneven land and sandy soils** where flooding would waste water, and crops such as wheat, pulses, vegetables and tea.

Almost nothing is lost to evaporation or runoff, and weeds between rows get no water. It suits fruit, sugarcane and vegetables in dry areas. Sprinkler irrigation sprays water over the crop like rain. It suits uneven land and sandy soil, where flooding the field would waste most of the water.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much water does drip save?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A crop needs 4500 m³ of water per hectare at its roots (illustrative). Flooding delivers only 50% of applied water to the roots, drip 90%. How much water must be applied by each method, and what is saved?

**Step 1. Flooding.** Applied $= \frac{4500}{0.5} = 9000$ m³.

**Step 2. Drip.** Applied $= \frac{4500}{0.9} = 5000$ m³.

**Step 3. Saving.** $9000 - 5000 = 4000$ m³ per hectare — water that could irrigate more land or stay in the aquifer.

notes.title: Water Resources — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Surface water and groundwater
sections.body_md:
- **Surface water:** rivers, lakes, ponds, tanks, reservoirs; fed by rain and (in the north) snowmelt.
- **Groundwater:** water that has soaked into the ground and fills pores and cracks below the **water table**, in **aquifers**; reached by wells and tube wells; recharged by rain and seepage from rivers and canals.
- **Northern plains:** perennial snow-fed rivers; porous alluvium with plentiful, shallow groundwater.
- **Peninsula:** seasonal rain-fed rivers; hard crystalline rock with limited groundwater; tanks.

key_terms.definition_md: The upper level of the saturated zone below the ground, under which rocks are full of water.
A layer of porous rock or sediment that holds and yields groundwater.

visual.alt: Table contrasting surface water and groundwater

sections.heading: 2. Need for water conservation
sections.body_md:
- Rain is **seasonal** (three to four monsoon months) and **uneven** across regions.
- **Rising demand:** population, irrigation, industry, cities.
- **Over-use of groundwater:** water tables falling in parts of Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu.
- **Pollution** of rivers and lakes by sewage, industrial waste and farm chemicals.
- **Recurring droughts** when the monsoon fails.
- **Ways to conserve:** rainwater harvesting, efficient irrigation (drip, sprinkler), less thirsty crops, recycling waste water, fixing leaks, protecting lakes and rivers from pollution.

key_terms.definition_md: Using water carefully and protecting its sources so that enough clean water remains for the future.

visual.alt: Table of causes of water scarcity and remedies

sections.heading: 3. Rainwater harvesting
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** collecting and storing rain where it falls, for use or to recharge groundwater.
- **Rooftop harvesting:** roof → gutter → down pipe → first-flush device → filter (sand, gravel) → storage tank → overflow to a recharge pit or well → aquifer.
- **Other methods:** recharge pits and trenches, check dams, percolation tanks, farm ponds, reviving village tanks.
- **Importance:** raises the water table; water in the dry season; less street flooding in cities; less soil erosion; better groundwater quality (dilutes fluoride and salts); cheap; people's participation.
- **Harvest (litres)** = roof area (m²) × rainfall (mm) × runoff coefficient.

key_terms.definition_md: Collecting and storing rainwater for use or for recharging groundwater.
A pit filled with gravel and sand through which harvested water soaks down to the groundwater.
The fraction of rain falling on a surface that can actually be collected.

visual.alt: Table of the stages of rooftop harvesting

sections.heading: 4. Irrigation: need, wells and tube wells
sections.body_md:
- **Need:** seasonal, uncertain and uneven rain; dry rabi season; thirsty crops (rice, sugarcane); multiple cropping; high-yielding seeds; porous soils.
- **Wells:** dug to the water table; water lifted by hand, Persian wheel or pump; cheap, owned by farmers; small areas.
- **Tube wells:** deep bores with electric or diesel pumps; large supplies.
- Wells and tube wells are the **leading source of irrigation** (as of the early 2020s): Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat.
- **Why tube wells in the northern plains:** soft alluvium easy to bore; plentiful recharged groundwater; electricity; flat land; high demand.

key_terms.definition_md: The artificial supply of water to crops.
A deep, narrow bore into an aquifer from which water is lifted by a power-driven pump.

visual.alt: Table comparing wells and tube wells

sections.heading: 5. Tank irrigation
sections.body_md:
- **Tank:** natural or man-made depression (often an earth embankment across a stream) that stores rainwater.
- **Where:** Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh.
- **Why in the peninsula:** hard impervious rock (little groundwater); seasonal rain-fed rivers; undulating land with natural hollows; rain concentrated in a short season; small scattered fields.
- **Drawbacks:** dry up in droughts; silting; evaporation loss; occupy fertile land; small command area.

key_terms.definition_md: A small reservoir, natural or made by an embankment, that stores rainwater for irrigation.

visual.alt: Table of advantages and drawbacks of tanks

sections.heading: 6. Canals and modern irrigation
sections.body_md:
- **Inundation canals:** from a river without a barrage; water only in floods (rainy season); unreliable.
- **Perennial canals:** from a barrage, weir or dam; water all year; northern plains (Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh) and southern deltas.
- **Examples:** Indira Gandhi Canal, Upper Ganga Canal, Western Yamuna Canal, Sirhind Canal.
- **Disadvantages:** waterlogging; salinity and alkalinity (reh, kallar); mosquitoes and malaria; seepage and evaporation losses; costly; only on flat land; tail-end farms short of water.
- **Drip irrigation:** water drop by drop at the roots through pipes and emitters; least waste; orchards, sugarcane, vegetables in dry areas.
- **Sprinkler irrigation:** water sprayed like rain; uneven land, sandy soils; wheat, pulses, vegetables, tea.

key_terms.definition_md: A canal taken from a river at a barrage or dam, which flows throughout the year.
A canal taken from a river without a barrage, which carries water only when the river is in flood.
Supplying water drop by drop directly to the root zone of plants through pipes and emitters.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between perennial canals and inundation canals.

answer.model_answer_md: Perennial canals are taken from rivers at a barrage, weir or dam that holds the water up, so they supply water throughout the year. Disease: stagnant water in waterlogged fields and canal edges breeds mosquitoes, spreading malaria. Uneven supply: farms near the head of the canal take more than their share, while tail-end farms get little.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Surface water flows or stands on the land, as in rivers, lakes and reservoirs — for example, the Krishna. Groundwater fills the pores of rocks below the water table and is reached by wells — for example, the tube wells of Haryana.

(b) The deep, porous alluvium stores large amounts of water; it is recharged by monsoon rain and by seepage from perennial snow-fed rivers and canals.

(c) Rain from the roof flows through gutters and a down pipe; the first-flush device discards dirty water and a filter cleans the rest; overflow from the storage tank goes into a recharge pit filled with gravel and sand, from which it soaks down to the aquifer and raises the water table.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Rain falls mainly in a few monsoon months and unevenly across regions; demand from a growing population, farms and industry is rising while groundwater is being over-drawn (pollution also reduces usable water).

(b) Recharge pits or trenches; check dams or percolation tanks across streams (also farm ponds, reviving village tanks).

(c) It recharges groundwater and revives wells; it provides water in the dry season; it reduces runoff, urban flooding and soil erosion (and improves groundwater quality at low cost).

(d) Build check dams and farm ponds to hold monsoon runoff so that it soaks in; use drip or sprinkler irrigation, which delivers water to the roots with little waste; grow less thirsty crops such as millets and pulses instead of sugarcane.

questions.solution_md: Reasons; methods; advantages; measures for a dry village.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give two reasons why irrigation is necessary in India. [2]

(b) Distinguish between a well and a tube well. [2]

(c) Explain three reasons why tube wells are widely used in the northern plains. [3]

(d) Explain three reasons why tank irrigation is important in peninsular India. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Rain is seasonal, falling mainly in three to four months, so dry-season crops need water; the monsoon is uncertain and uneven, and some crops such as rice and sugarcane need much water.

(b) A well is a pit dug down to the water table; water is lifted by hand, a Persian wheel or a small pump, and it waters a small area. A tube well is a deep, narrow bore into the aquifer with a powerful electric or diesel pump, and it supplies much more water.

(c) Soft, deep alluvium is easy to bore; it holds plentiful groundwater, recharged by rain and snow-fed rivers and canals; rural electricity, flat land and a large demand from intensive farming make pumping worthwhile.

(d) Hard crystalline rock holds little groundwater, so wells yield little; rivers are rain-fed and seasonal, unfit for perennial canals; the undulating land has natural hollows that are easily made into tanks to store the monsoon rain.

questions.solution_md: Need; well and tube well; tube wells in the north; tanks in the south.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between perennial and inundation canals. [2]

(b) Name two perennial canals of India and the state that each serves. [2]

(c) State three disadvantages of canal irrigation. [3]

(d) Explain how drip and sprinkler irrigation save water, and name a type of farm or land suited to each. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Perennial canals start at a barrage, weir or dam and flow all year; inundation canals have no barrage and carry water only when the river is in flood.

(b) The Indira Gandhi Canal — Rajasthan; the Upper Ganga Canal — Uttar Pradesh (also the Western Yamuna Canal — Haryana; the Sirhind Canal — Punjab).

(c) Waterlogging from seepage and over-watering; salinity and alkalinity (reh, kallar) as waterlogged land dries; breeding of mosquitoes (also seepage losses, high cost, uneven supply to tail-end farms).

(d) Drip carries water in pipes and releases it drop by drop at the roots, so little is lost to evaporation or runoff — suited to orchards, vineyards and sugarcane in dry areas such as around Nashik. Sprinklers spray water evenly like rain, avoiding the seepage and runoff of flooding — suited to uneven land and sandy soils, as in parts of Rajasthan.

questions.solution_md: Canal types; examples; disadvantages; drip and sprinkler.

Study the illustrative data. Share of irrigated area by source — District A: wells and tube wells 72%, canals 24%, tanks 1%, other 3%. District B: wells and tube wells 30%, canals 18%, tanks 42%, other 10%. A crop needs 4500 m³ of water per hectare at its roots; flooding is 50% efficient and drip 90% efficient.

(a) Which district relies mainly on tanks? In which part of India is it likely to be? [2]

(b) In District A, what share of the irrigated area is watered by sources other than wells and tube wells? [2]

(c) Calculate the water that must be applied per hectare by flooding and by drip, and the saving. [3]

(d) The water table in District A is falling. Recommend three measures, with reasons. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) District B (tanks 42%); the hard-rock plateau of Tamil Nadu, Telangana or Karnataka.

(b) $24 + 1 + 3 = 28$%.

(c) Flooding $= \frac{4500}{0.5} = 9000$ m³; drip $= \frac{4500}{0.9} = 5000$ m³; saving $= 9000 - 5000 = 4000$ m³ per hectare.

(d) Switch from flooding to drip or sprinkler irrigation, which needs far less water for the same crop; build recharge pits, check dams and rooftop harvesting so that more monsoon rain soaks into the aquifer; grow less thirsty crops in part of the area and avoid pumping for a dry-season rice crop.

questions.solution_md: District B, southern plateau; 28%; 9000, 5000, saving 4000 m³; drip, recharge, crop change.
